newsitem.title: UK: UK Tory pretender Hague benefits from Blair factor.
newsitem.headline: UK Tory pretender Hague benefits from Blair factor.

text.p: William Hague, the very young pretender to the leadership of Britain's Conservative Party, has benefited greatly from the "Blair Effect" -- the idea that youth and inexperience is a vote-winner.
At just 36, Hague would be the youngest Conservative leader since the early 19th century if he beats four other contenders in a party poll that begins on June 10.

Many members of parliament believe Hague could provide a double advantage to a party still licking its wounds after its thrashing at a general election on May 1 which swept Labour to power after 18 years of Conservative rule.

He will cancel out the youthful image of Labour's Tony Blair, 44 and the most popular prime minister since opinion polls began, and mark a break from the "old" Conservative government so comprehensively beaten at the election.

"We must take this once in a lifetime opportunity to make a fresh start -- a fresh start in our organisation, membership and image, and to rethink some of our policies," Hague told party activists last month.
Although Hague, the youngest cabinet minister for 50 years when he became Welsh Secretary in 1995, is a relative newcomer to the political spotlight, he has been a media star since 1977.

At that year's Conservative party conference the 16-year-old Hague impressed Margaret Thatcher and brought the 5,000 delegates to their feet with a rousing speech calling on the then-Labour government to "roll back the frontiers of the state".
He graduated from Oxford with a first class degree in philosophy, politics and economics, and initially became a press officer for oil giant Shell before joining a management consultancy.
It was no surprise when Hague decided to contest the Richmond seat in north Yorkshire in 1989, the last time the Conservatives won a parliamentary by-election.

Hague's rise to cabinet status, via ministerial posts in the social security department, was swift but left few outside or inside parliament with any idea of what he stood for or which wing of the party he represented.
Since announcing his candidacy, Hague has shown himself to be on the "Eurosceptic" side in the key argument over closer links with the European Union.

"We need to be in Europe but not run by Europe" is a favourite Hague soundbite, but like his views on many subjects, the firm-sounding phrases are not backed up by much substance. His political beliefs appear not yet sufficiently formed for him to have earned any enemies.
"He is a man of quality yet a man without qualities; his political personality is not just indistinct but undetectable," said former Conservative MP George Walden.
"Hague is a nice fellow. So nice that it is hard to think of anything he has said or done to which anyone could take exception," Walden said in a newspaper article.

Hague's smile and friendly, unthreatening manner are a sharp contrast to most of the other leadership contenders and seen as another asset by many Conservatives, looking nervously at the impact achieved by Blair.

He appears to be appreciated by Conservative grass-root supporters, but initial enthusiasm for the Hague bid has waned slightly in recent days -- he is now second favourite behind former finance minister Kenneth Clarke.
Hard-headed MPs, the only ones to vote in the party election, appear to see Clarke's experience and parliamentary polish as the more attractive option.
Hague maintains "I've finally got past the point where people say 'Oh, you're that teenager'", but for many MPs the prematurely balding Hague remains a youngster still untested under fire.

He took a step towards updating this image by announcing shortly before the election he would marry Ffion Jenkins, a 29-year-old high-flyer he met in the Welsh department when she taught him the words to the Welsh national anthem.
